passages.happening:
“I commend to you our sister Phoebe, a servant of the church in Cenchrea” (verse 1).

“Welcome her in the Lord in a manner worthy of the saints, and assist her with anything she may need from you. For she has been a great help to many people, including me” (verse 2).
passages.hearers:
A letter of recommendation was a common thing in the Roman world. A traveller carried a letter from a friend that introduced him to people who could give him a bed, meals and help. These two verses are such a letter, in miniature.

Cenchrea was the eastern port of Corinth, where Paul was writing. The letter does not say Phoebe carried it to Rome. But a letter like this one usually introduced the person who brought it, so most readers think she very likely did. If so, she would have been the one to read it aloud or explain it to the house churches.

Paul calls her ‘our sister’: a member of God's family. He calls her a ‘servant’ of the church. The Greek word is diakonos. It can mean a servant or helper in general, and it is also the word for the church office of deacon (Philippians 1:1; 1 Timothy 3:8). Readers differ on which Paul means here.

‘A great help’ translates the Greek prostatis. The word was used of patrons, people of means who supported others with money, a home and protection. Patrons were at the heart of Roman society. Phoebe was very likely a woman of some wealth who used it for the church, and for Paul himself.
passages.ot:
Paul's call to welcome a traveller ‘in a manner worthy of the saints’ stands in the long line of hospitality in Israel's Scriptures. Abraham ran to welcome strangers at his tent (Genesis 18:1-8). The law said, “So you also must love the foreigner, since you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt” (Deuteronomy 10:19).

The Old Testament also honours women who supported God's servants from their own means. A wealthy woman of Shunem, who saw that Elisha was “a holy man of God” (2 Kings 4:9), built a room for him on her roof. Luke tells of women who supported Jesus' work “out of their own means” (Luke 8:3).
passages.hard:
Was Phoebe a deacon, and what does that mean for women's roles in the church? The word diakonos can be read either way, and the book page says readers differ. Many churches have had women deacons, from early times to today; others have not, and some keep the office of deacon for men.

Christians who hold different views both read this passage carefully. These views are held by faithful believers, and these notes do not choose between them.

Complementarian Christians believe that men and women are equal in worth before God, and that God has given them different roles in the church and the home, with the office of pastor or elder, and teaching the gathered church with that authority, given to qualified men. Many of them gladly see Phoebe as a deacon or a trusted servant of the church, and honour her as a patron and leader in service, without reading her as an elder.

Egalitarian Christians believe that men and women are equal in worth and that every role in the church, including pastor and teacher, is open to both, as God gifts them. They point to Phoebe as evidence: Paul gives her a church title, commends her to a whole city's churches, and calls her his own patron.

Both sides agree on much: Phoebe was a respected servant of Christ, trusted by Paul, and honoured by him in the first line of his greetings.
passages.asks: Paul asks the Romans to help Phoebe ‘with anything she may need’. Think of someone who serves your church quietly, with money, a home or time. Ask how you could help them, and thank them by name this week.

passages.happening:
Paul sends greetings by name. “Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus” (verse 3), who risked their lives for him, and the church that meets in their house (verses 4-5). He greets Epenetus, the first convert in the province of Asia, and Mary, who worked very hard (verses 5-6).

“Greet Andronicus and Junia, my fellow countrymen and fellow prisoners. They are outstanding among the apostles, and they were in Christ before I was” (verse 7).

The names go on: Ampliatus, Urbanus, Stachys, Apelles, those of the household of Aristobulus, Herodion, those of the household of Narcissus who are in the Lord, Tryphena and Tryphosa, ‘women who have worked hard in the Lord’, Persis, Rufus and his mother, ‘who has been a mother to me as well’ (verses 8-13). Then two more groups with ‘the brothers with them’ and ‘all the saints with them’ (verses 14-15).

“Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the churches of Christ send you greetings” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
This list is easy to skip. It should not be. It is a picture of a real church in real houses.

Prisca and Aquila were a Jewish couple, tentmakers by trade. They had left Rome when Claudius ordered the Jews out of the city, met Paul in Corinth, worked with him, and had a church meeting in their home in Ephesus (Acts 18:2; 1 Corinthians 16:19). Now they were back in Rome, with a church in their house again. Paul names Prisca first, as Luke does twice in Acts 18.

Andronicus and Junia were Jewish, ‘fellow countrymen’, and had been in prison with Paul at some point. They believed in Christ before he did, so they were among the very early believers.

Many of the names were common among slaves and freed slaves in Rome, such as Ampliatus, Urbanus, Stachys and Hermes. That does not prove that each of these people was a slave. But it suggests that many in the Roman church were of low standing. ‘The household of Aristobulus’ and ‘the household of Narcissus’ probably mean the slaves and freed slaves of great houses, some of whom were believers. Some have tried to identify these households with famous men of the time, but that cannot be confirmed.

The list includes Jews and Gentiles, women and men, perhaps slaves and owners. Ten women are named or mentioned in the list. In this church they all greeted one another as family.

The ‘holy kiss’ was the greeting of family and friends. Among believers it said: we are one family now, across every line that divided Rome.
passages.ot:
Paul calls Andronicus, Junia and Herodion his ‘fellow countrymen’: Israelites, like him. The church in Rome was rooted in Israel, as Paul's picture of the olive tree said (11:17-18).

Rufus may be the son of Simon of Cyrene, whom the soldiers forced to carry Jesus' cross: Mark calls Simon “the father of Alexander and Rufus” (Mark 15:21), and Mark's Gospel is often linked with Rome. But Rufus was a common name, and this is uncertain.

Behind the greeting of family stands the Old Testament's picture of one people from many nations. God promised Abraham, “all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:3). This list of names from many places is one small fulfilment of that promise.
passages.hard:
Who was Junia, and was she an apostle? This is one of the book page's hard passages.

Junia was a common Latin name for a woman. A man's name ‘Junias’ has not been found in any ancient source. The early Christian writers who mention her, almost without exception, took her to be a woman, and most scholars today agree. For some centuries a number of translations printed a man's name; most now print ‘Junia’.

The harder question is what ‘outstanding among the apostles’ means. The Greek can be read ‘outstanding among the apostles’, meaning they were apostles of note, or ‘well known to the apostles’, meaning the apostles thought highly of them. Scholars argue both, and the BSB prints the first.

And ‘apostle’ may not mean one of the Twelve. The word means one who is sent. Paul uses it of messengers sent by churches (2 Corinthians 8:23, where the BSB has ‘messengers’).

Complementarian Christians, who hold the office of pastor or elder for qualified men, often read the phrase as ‘well known to the apostles’, or take ‘apostle’ here as a travelling messenger, not a church office of authority. Egalitarian Christians, who hold every role open to both, see in Junia a woman honoured as an apostle, and in Phoebe and Prisca women in recognised ministry. These notes do not choose. Both sides agree that Paul honoured these women by name, and that women were at the heart of his work.
passages.asks: Paul knew these people by name, and what each had done. Write down the names of believers who have helped you in your faith. Thank God for each one. Then greet one of them this week, and tell them what they did.

passages.happening:
“Now I urge you, brothers, to watch out for those who create divisions and obstacles that are contrary to the teaching you have learned. Turn away from them” (verse 17).

Such people do not serve Christ but their own appetites, and “By smooth talk and flattery they deceive the hearts of the naive” (verse 18).

Everyone has heard of the Romans' obedience, and Paul rejoices. “But I want you to be wise about what is good and innocent about what is evil” (verse 19).

“The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
After the warm greetings comes a sharp warning. It may seem out of place. But it fits. Paul has just pictured a church held together by love. Those who ‘create divisions’ threaten exactly that.

Paul does not name these people, and readers do not know who they were. They were not the ‘weak’ and ‘strong’ of chapter 14, whom Paul told to accept one another. These were people who taught against ‘the teaching you have learned’: the gospel itself. Paul says to notice them and keep away from them.

‘Their own appetites’ means their own desires: for money, status, a following. ‘Smooth talk and flattery’ is how they win people. The ‘naive’ are those who trust too easily.

‘Wise about what is good and innocent about what is evil’ means to be skilled at doing good, and to have nothing to do with evil.

‘The God of peace’ is a striking title just after a warning about division. Peace is God's work. And the promise that Satan will be crushed ‘soon’ was meant to steady a small church in a hostile city.
passages.ot:
Verse 20 echoes the first promise in the Bible. After the serpent deceived Eve, God said to it, “He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel” (Genesis 3:15). Christians have long read that promise of Christ's victory over evil. Paul says God will crush Satan ‘under your feet’: his people will share the victory.

Wisdom literature warns against flatterers too: “A lying tongue hates those it crushes, and a flattering mouth causes ruin” (Proverbs 26:28).
passages.hard: Does ‘turn away from them’ mean believers should cut off anyone they disagree with? No. This chapter must be read with chapter 14, where Paul told believers who disagree about food and days to accept one another and not judge. The warning here is about people who teach against the gospel itself and stir up division for their own gain. Christians differ, as the note on 14:1-12 says, on where exactly the line between the gospel and matters of conscience falls. But Paul's warning is not a license to treat every disagreement as a reason to separate. It is a call to guard the church from those who would tear it apart.
passages.asks: Paul wants believers to be wise about good and innocent about evil. Ask where flattery has an easy way into your life. Then ask whether you are building up your church's peace, or quietly working against it.

passages.happening:
Now those with Paul send their greetings. “Timothy, my fellow worker, sends you greetings, as do Lucius, Jason, and Sosipater, my fellow countrymen” (verse 21).

Then a new voice. “I, Tertius, who wrote down this letter, greet you in the Lord” (verse 22).

“Gaius, who has hosted me and all the church, sends you greetings. Erastus, the city treasurer, sends you greetings, as does our brother Quartus” (verse 23).

There is no verse 24 in the Berean Standard Bible. The oldest copies of Romans do not have it.
passages.hearers:
Timothy was one of Paul's closest helpers. In 1 Timothy he is called “my true child in the faith” (1 Timothy 1:2). Lucius, Jason and Sosipater were Jewish believers with Paul in Corinth.

Tertius is the man who wrote the letter down as Paul spoke it. Using a trained writer for a letter was common in the Roman world. For a moment he puts down Paul's words and adds his own. It is a reminder that this letter was made by real people in a real room.

Gaius was very likely the Gaius whom Paul baptized at Corinth (1 Corinthians 1:14). He was host to Paul and to ‘all the church’, so his house was big enough for the believers of Corinth to gather.

Erastus was ‘the city treasurer’, a man of some rank. A stone with the name Erastus was found at Corinth in 1929, but whether it names the same man is disputed.

Verse 24, a closing blessing found in some later copies, is missing from the oldest. That is why the BSB leaves the number empty. Nothing in the letter's teaching depends on it.
passages.ot: Blessing one another is an old habit of God's people. The priests of Israel were given words to bless the people: “May the LORD bless you and keep you” (Numbers 6:24). Paul's greetings from Jewish and Gentile believers alike, in Corinth, to Jewish and Gentile believers in Rome, show God's promise to bless the nations through Abraham's family at work.
passages.asks: Tertius did the quiet work of writing the letter down. Think of someone whose quiet work makes your church's life possible. Ask how you might add your own greeting to theirs, and thank them.

passages.t: ‘To the only wise God be glory’
passages.happening: Paul ends with praise. “Now to Him who is able to strengthen you by my gospel and by the proclamation of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery concealed for ages past” (verse 25), “but now revealed and made known through the writings of the prophets by the command of the eternal God, in order to lead all nations to the obedience that comes from faith” (verse 26), “to the only wise God be glory forever through Jesus Christ! Amen” (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
This is a doxology, a short hymn of praise to God. It gathers up the whole letter.

‘My gospel’ is the good news Paul has explained in sixteen chapters. ‘The mystery concealed for ages past’ is God's plan, kept hidden for a long time and now made known: that through Christ, Gentiles and Jews together would be one people of God.

‘Through the writings of the prophets’. Paul has quoted Israel's Scriptures again and again in this letter. The good news was not new in the sense of strange. It had been promised all along.

And the last words before the praise are the words Paul used at the start: ‘the obedience that comes from faith’, among ‘all nations’. In chapter 1 he said that his calling was “to call all those among the Gentiles to the obedience that comes from faith” (Romans 1:5). The letter ends where it began.

‘The only wise God’ recalls the end of chapter 11: “O, the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Romans 11:33). The argument has led, once again, to worship.
passages.ot:
‘The writings of the prophets’ points to the whole of Israel's Scriptures. Paul has quoted the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms throughout Romans, from Habakkuk's “The righteous will live by faith” (Romans 1:17) to Isaiah's “in Him the Gentiles will put their hope” (Romans 15:12).

The phrase ‘the eternal God’ goes back to Moses: “The eternal God is your dwelling place, and underneath are the everlasting arms” (Deuteronomy 33:27). And the praise of God's wisdom echoes Israel's wisdom books, where wisdom belongs to God first of all.
passages.hard: Did Paul write these closing words where they stand? The old manuscripts, the hand-copied texts of the New Testament, show something unusual here. In many of the oldest and best copies, these words come at the end of chapter 16, as in the BSB. In others they come after 14:23. In one very early papyrus they come after 15:33. A few later copies leave them out altogether. Scholars explain this in different ways, for example that shorter copies of Romans once circulated. Most editors today print the words here, at the end of the letter, because early copies from many places have them here. Some scholars think the words are Paul's own; others think they were added early. Nothing in the letter's teaching depends on where they stand. The book page says the same.
passages.asks:
Romans began and ended with ‘the obedience that comes from faith’. Ask what one act of obedience your faith is asking of you now. Then read verses 25 to 27 aloud as your own praise.

Where next? The site's book page on Romans sets out the letter as a whole: its setting, its argument, and the questions readers bring to it. And Paul's other letters, beginning with 1 Corinthians, carry the same gospel into the life of other churches.
